mechanism_fit: M15, a faulty fallback path. BigFraction.doubleValue has a short normal branch at the top, `numerator.doubleValue() / denominator.doubleValue()`, which is correct and is all that any existing caller needs. It also has a fallback inside `if (Double.isNaN(result))`, which recovers when both BigInteger parts are larger than Double.MAX_VALUE. The fault is only in that fallback: the shift that brings the parts back into range is computed from numerator.bitLength() alone. It shows only when both parts are above 2^1024 and the denominator is at least two bits longer than the numerator. That means a reduced fraction below about 1/2. The trigger never calls the fallback by name. It builds an exact two-state Markov transition matrix of BigFraction values, raises it to several powers with FieldMatrix.power (public behaviour), and compares each entry's doubleValue() with RealMatrix.power on doubles. Steps 1, 2, 10, 100 and 1000 take the normal branch and agree. Only n = 2000 reaches the fallback. There the off-diagonal entry (2^2000-1)/2^2001 becomes 0.0 while the diagonal entry (2^2000+1)/2^2001 still gives 0.5. A reader who trusts the normal branch, which looks obviously correct, is drawn to the matrix power or multiply code or to the BigFraction arithmetic as the cause.
gold: org.apache.commons.math3.fraction.BigFraction::doubleValue (src/main/java/org/apache/commons/math3/fraction/BigFraction.java). Edit: `int shift = Math.max(numerator.bitLength(), denominator.bitLength()) - FastMath.getExponent(Double.MAX_VALUE);` -> `int shift = numerator.bitLength() - FastMath.getExponent(Double.MAX_VALUE);`. The minimal repair restores the max of both bit lengths.
ownership_reason: BigFraction.doubleValue owns the fault. Its fallback comment says it must shift 'numerator and/or denominator' to 'put them in range'. The variant computes the shift from numerator.bitLength() only. So when the reduced denominator is two or more bits longer than the numerator and both parts are above 2^1024, the shifted denominator is still at least 2^1024, converts to Infinity, and the result collapses to 0.0. The sibling BigFraction.floatValue runs the same fallback with Math.max(numerator.bitLength(), denominator.bitLength()). The passing MATH-744 tests (testDoubleValueForLargeNumeratorAndDenominator and testFloatValueForLargeNumeratorAndDenominator) cover the fallback only for a numerator larger than the denominator (value 5), and the variant still passes them. The competitors produce the exact fraction. For P = [[3/4,1/4],[1/4,3/4]], P^n has entries (2^n plus or minus 1)/2^(n+1). The BigFraction constructor reduces every result to lowest terms, so each value has a single representation. AbstractFieldMatrix.power is checked against repeated multiplication by the passing FieldMatrixImplTest.testPower, and it mirrors AbstractRealMatrix.power, which supplies the 0.5 reference values in the trigger itself. BigFractionTest.testAdd and testMultiply cover the arithmetic. No edit to power, multiply or add can change what doubleValue receives without breaking the exact-arithmetic tests. G9 confirms this: none of the 5 declared one-line decoy edits makes the trigger pass.
trigger: org.apache.commons.math3.linear.FieldMatrixImplTest::testTwoStateChainExactAndFloatingStepsAgree. It builds the exact matrix FieldMatrix<BigFraction> [[3/4,1/4],[1/4,3/4]] and the same matrix as a RealMatrix of doubles. For n in {1, 2, 10, 100, 1000, 2000} it asserts assertEquals(approximate.power(n).getEntry(i,j), exact.power(n).getEntry(i,j).doubleValue(), 1e-12). The only new import is org.apache.commons.math3.fraction.BigFraction.

concerns: 1) Decisive evidence for the gold is fairly close by: the sibling floatValue and the fallback's own comment ('shift them'). A model that realises the matrix entries are fractions of about 2000 bits will probably find the fault quickly. The M15 difficulty rests on a model trusting the normal division and not noticing how large the entries are. 2) The trigger calls doubleValue() directly on matrix entries. I chose that deliberately: routing it through MatrixUtils.bigFractionMatrixToRealMatrix would hide the call better, but then a one-line converter workaround (for example converting through bigDecimalValue) could absorb the fault. With the direct call, ownership stays clean. 3) Two decoy methods are both named `multiply` (in AbstractFieldMatrix and BigFraction); each spec entry has its class, and BigFraction::multiply carries a decl. 4) The failure message does not say which n failed, so a solver must work out that only n = 2000 reaches the fallback.
